analysis.one_liner: Makes OPEC-style foreign oil cartels subject to U.S. antitrust lawsuits by removing their sovereign immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill to allow antitrust suits against foreign oil cartels died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The NOPEC bill would change U.S. antitrust law so that foreign governments that band together to restrict oil production or fix oil prices—a practice OPEC members engage in—could be sued in American courts for violating the Sherman Act. Normally foreign countries are immune from U.S. lawsuits; the bill would strip that immunity for oil cartel conduct and let the Attorney General enforce it. The bill never received any committee action or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, who would benefit if the threat of antitrust suits deterred foreign oil producers from coordinating production cuts and price increases that raise gasoline, heating fuel, and goods-transport costs. American oil refiners and downstream users of crude also stand to gain from more competitive pricing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers paying gas and fuel prices

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Sherman Act to make it illegal for foreign states to collectively limit oil production or fix oil prices when the effect reaches U.S. markets.
It strips foreign states of sovereign immunity so they can actually be sued, and gives the Attorney General sole authority to bring those cases in federal court.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign state-owned oil producers, who would face lawsuits and potentially large judgments in U.S. courts for cartel behavior, and foreign governments whose diplomatic relations with the U.S. could suffer as a result. Some economists argue consumers could ultimately bear retaliation costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes sovereign immunity for foreign states in oil cartel cases, which would let U.S. courts sit in judgment of foreign governments' official energy policies—a step that could provoke retaliation, such as asset seizures of American firms abroad or reduced cooperation on energy and security matters.
It is unclear how effectively U.S. antitrust law can be enforced against foreign states controlling their own natural resources, so the practical benefit for pump prices is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—deterrence of foreign oil cartel behavior that raises American fuel prices—could be substantial, and the Attorney General's sole enforcement authority is a real check against a flood of opportunistic suits. The cost is diplomatic: foreign oil producers would view a U.S. court's power to strip their immunity and seize assets as grounds to retaliate against American interests, which is the objection that has kept this bill from advancing for years. On the merits for consumers, the bill's design is sound; the risk is foreign-policy blowback rather than domestic harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 7, 2023 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never left committee, never got a hearing, and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign oil-producing states keep their immunity from U.S. antitrust suits, and no one else gains materially.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors including the Judiciary chair.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor but the committee he chaired took no action on the bill.

for.name: Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, no markup, no vote—so it never advanced.

against.name: Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; as floor scheduler, no bill leaves committee into a floor vote without leadership action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsors were bipartisan—two Republicans and two Democrats—and similar versions have drawn wide bipartisan support in past Congresses, but the bill still died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Foreign state-owned oil producers (OPEC and similar cartels)
industries.note: The bill would expose foreign state oil producers to antitrust suits and judgments in U.S. courts for collective production and pricing decisions, removing the sovereign immunity that currently shields them.

Lower crude prices from cartel discipline would cut into producers' revenue, though refiners and downstream firms could benefit from cheaper input costs. No direct action is taken against domestic producers.
